newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Cambodia seen reverting to civil war days.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia seen reverting to civil war days.

text.p: Cambodia's political map is taking on an eerie familiarity, and analysts say this dismays friends and neighbours involved in ending the country's two-decade long civil war.
"It's like back to the future. It's scary," one Western diplomat said.

Cambodia's Second Prime Minister Hun Sen is effectively in control of the capital Phnom Penh and well entrenched in the south and east of the country after his virtual coup at the weekend, diplomats noted.

Forces loyal to his ousted rival, First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranardiddh, are regrouping in their traditional strongholds in the north and northwest of the country. The remnants of the Khmer Rouge -- as well as its apparently repudiated leader, the reviled Pol Pot -- are still holed up in jungles in the west and the far north.
That's pretty much how things stood in 1991 when the Paris Peace Accords were signed, paving the way for elections and an end to a civil war that killed more than one million people.
Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party won the 1993 elections, supervised by the United Nations at a cost of $2 billion.

But Hun Sen's communist party, which had been in power in Phnom Penh with Vietnam's backing for more than a decade, was given a share of power in Cambodia to reflect the fact that his troops far outnumbered Ranardiddh's.
Their uneasy cohabitation finally dissolved when Hun Sen ousted his rival last weekend, accusing Ranariddh of beefing up his forces with defecting Khmer Rouge insurgents.
At least 58 people were killed and up to 200 wounded in the ouster, most of them civilians. A senior interior ministry official loyal to Ranariddh was executed, and other loyalists are in hiding.
In another echo of the past, the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) called an emergency meeting on Cambodia in Kuala Lumpur on Thursday.
ASEAN has had plenty of experience with that. In the
1980s, most of its meetings were dominated by discussions of Vietnam's invasion and subsequent occupation of Cambodia beginning in 1978.
ASEAN in those days backed a coalition of guerrillas led by King Norodom Sihanouk and including Ranariddh, his son, and the Khmer Rouge.
The coalition was arrayed against Hun Sen, who was installed in power in Phnom Penh after the Vietnamese swarmed across the border in 1978 to get rid of Pol Pot and his "killing fields" regime.
Pol Pot, who has not been publicly sighted in years, is still said to be wasting away from illness in some remote jungle near the Thai border. More than a decade ago, he was also reported near death.

Then, as now, Sihanouk spends much of his time in Beijing, where he has a palace, recovering from various illnesses. Also then, as now, China's interest in Cambodia's affairs worries Southeast Asian nations. "It's like deja vu," said Abdul Razak Baginda, executive director of the Malaysian Strategic Research Centre. "When Vietnam invaded, Sihanouk was in China and Hun Sen was installed in Phnom Penh."
"ASEAN is well aware of China's interest. People forget China fought a border war with Vietnam (in 1979) after that to teach it a lesson," he said.
But there are some key differences.
ASEAN has much more clout today than it did a decade ago.
Cambodia is eager for membership, and the possible economic and political benefits that come with it, as donor fatigue about Phnom Penh sets in with the international community.
Vietnam, for so long at odds with ASEAN over Cambodia, is now a member itself. Hun Sen may not be able to count as much on Hanoi's support, analysts said.
Although Hun Sen was in Vietnam last week before making his move against Ranariddh, a Vietnam foreign ministry spokesman said it was a personal visit and he did not meet any Vietnamese leaders.
